summary: Describes a way to avoid blackholing traffic when the IGP is working on a link where LDP is not, by making routers keep the link from being preferred until LDP is ready. This matters for networks relying on LDP label switched paths, for example MPLS VPNs. This is an informational document, later updated by RFC 6138.

plainLanguage.summary: When a road is open to cars but its truck lane is not ready, only cars should use it. This document keeps all traffic off such a link until the label switching side is ready too, so nothing is lost.

questions: why does mpls traffic get blackholed
what is the maximum ospf link cost
how to avoid blackholing when ldp is down
subtitle: How to keep IP traffic off a link where routing works but label switching does not, without changing any protocol.

tldr.problem: A link can be carrying IGP traffic while LDP is not working on it. IP traffic still uses the link, but labeled traffic such as MPLS VPN traffic is blackholed.
tldr.mechanism: While LDP is not fully operational on a link, the IGP advertises that link at its maximum cost, so transit traffic avoids it even though the link stays in the topology.
tldr.outcome: Labeled traffic is steered to other paths until LDP is ready. The change is local to the router and needs no protocol changes.

today: RFC 5443 is an Informational document. It has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 6138 and RFC 10041, so read those alongside it.

sections.title: The Blackhole Problem
sections.content:
LDP (RFC 5036) builds MPLS label switched paths (LSPs) along the shortest path to a destination as computed by IP forwarding. In a common design an IGP such as OSPF (RFC 2328) or IS-IS (ISO 10589) runs on every link, and so does LDP, so the whole domain has matching IGP and LDP adjacencies.

Some services need a complete edge-to-edge MPLS path between provider-edge routers. The RFC names layer 2 and layer 3 VPNs. Every link on the IP shortest path must have an operational LDP session and the needed label bindings must have been exchanged over it. If even one link lacks an LDP session, a blackhole exists and services that depend on MPLS forwarding fail.

The RFC lists three causes: a configuration error, an implementation bug, or a link that has just come up and has an IGP adjacency while LDP has not yet formed a session or distributed all label bindings. LDP cannot repair this, because it is not a routing protocol and cannot send traffic down a different IGP path.
sections.plainLanguage: If one road on a delivery route is closed to trucks, the whole delivery fails, even though cars can still drive there. The trucks cannot pick another road on their own, so the network must keep them off that road in the first place.

sections.title: Raising the Link Cost Until LDP Is Ready
sections.content:
The problem exists because LDP follows IP forwarding decisions, but nothing couples a link's IGP state to its LDP state. The fix is to discourage the link from being used for IP forwarding while LDP is not fully operational on it.

The RFC notes a likeness to RFC 3137, which lets an OSPF router advertise that it should not be used for transit. One difference is that RFC 3137 raises costs on all of a stub router's links, while this mechanism works on one link at a time.

In detail, when LDP is not fully operational on a link, the IGP advertises the link at maximum cost. For OSPF that is LSInfinity, the 16-bit value 0xFFFF, as proposed in RFC 3137. For IS-IS the maximum metric value is 2^24-2 (0xFFFFFE). A link configured with 2^24-1, the maximum link metric of RFC 5305, is not advertised in the topology at all, so it cannot serve as a last resort. Keeping the link in the topology lets IP traffic still fall back on it during a massive failure.

LDP is fully operational on a link when an LDP hello adjacency exists, a matching LDP session is established with the peer at the far end, and all label bindings have been exchanged. A router generally cannot confirm the last point, so a simple strategy is a configurable hold-down timer before declaring LDP fully operational. The RFC defines no default, because label information base sizes and equipment capabilities vary widely. When LDP End-of-LIB (work in progress at the time) is implemented, the timer is not needed: receiving the End-of-LIB notification means the session is fully operational.

The mechanism brings no protocol changes and is a local implementation matter.
sections.plainLanguage: The router puts a very high toll on the half-ready link so nobody chooses it, but leaves the link open as a last resort. Once the truck lane is ready, the toll goes away. Deciding when it is ready may need a short wait, because the router cannot always tell by itself.

sections.title: When to Use It
sections.content:
The procedure suits networks where having working LDP-signaled MPLS LSPs and avoiding blackholes for MPLS traffic matters more than always choosing the best path for IP-forwarded traffic. The examples given are MPLS VPNs and BGP-free core designs, where traffic can pass through the core only when LDP forwarding state exists throughout.

Non-optimal IP forwarding happens only briefly after a link comes up, or while a real problem lasts. In the second case an implementation should raise network management alerts so the operator can fix the cause.

The mechanism also needs alternate paths with enough bandwidth, since the costed-out link carries no transit traffic. On a broadcast link with more than one IGP/LDP peer, the cost-out can apply only to the link as a whole, not to one peer, so a policy decision is needed on whether losing LDP to a single peer should divert traffic from all peers on that link.
sections.plainLanguage: This is worth doing when trucks matter more than taking the shortest route for cars, and only when there are other roads with room to spare. On a shared road, you cannot make it expensive for just one trucking company.

sections.title: Interaction with TE Tunnels
sections.content:
Some networks run LDP alongside RSVP-TE, which sets up traffic-engineered tunnels. TE tunnel path computation uses a separate TE link cost that the IGP floods in addition to the regular IP link cost. The RFC says the mechanism should be applied only to the IP link cost, to avoid needless TE tunnel reroutes.

LDP LSPs across a TE tunnel need a targeted LDP session between the tunnel endpoints. This is much like a regular link: when the tunnel is used for IP forwarding, its targeted LDP session must be operational. Raising the tunnel's IP cost while there is no operational session solves it. If there is no IGP adjacency over the tunnel and the tunnel is not advertised into the IGP as a link, this becomes a local matter for the tunnel headend router.
sections.plainLanguage: Reserved lanes keep their own price list. Only the normal price list is changed, so the reserved lanes are not rearranged for no reason.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A denial-of-service attack that takes LDP down on a link, or keeps it from becoming operational, could be one cause of LDP-related blackholing. The RFC does not address how to prevent LDP session failure. The mechanism prevents use of a link where LDP is down while the IGP is up, and assigning the maximum IGP cost on such a link is not expected to add new threats, since the operation is internal to the router so LDP and the IGP can communicate.

Making many LDP links unavailable at once is a threat, because dropping that much of the network can lose traffic when capacity is limited. Operational or implementation error may trigger it. The RFC treats these as general security issues and says implementors should follow current best security practice.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could break the truck lanes on purpose. This fix does not stop that, but it does not make things worse either. The bigger risk is many roads losing their truck lanes at once, leaving too little capacity for the remaining traffic.
